text:
Hey Melody - I'm not a convert but I do know a fair bit about the process. The Israeli Rabbinate's conversion is one of the most widely accepted in the world, but yes it is true that there will be communities that won't accept it - especially Haredi communities (including in Israel). Basically, there is no such thing as a conversion that is going to be recognised by every single Jew in the world - if you want to find someone who will not recognise your conversion, you will always be able find them. 

For example, the Syrian Jewish community is famous for not accepting converts at all. There is a story about a women who converted and wanted to marry someone from the community - Rav Ovadia Yosef himself wrote a letter saying her conversion is kosher to the highest standard. They still refused to accept her! 

My honest advice would be don't put yourself through another conversion based on a future fear about a community you don't currently live in, and whose country your future children may never even end up in. Unless you have been personally told by a rabbi from a specific community that you want to be a part of that your conversion is not accepted, I wouldn't assume there is a problem. Your children will be Jewish and the *vast majority of the Jewish world will* recognise that. Cross any remaining bridges if and when you actually come to them, rather than putting yourself through an enormously difficult process to solve a hypothetical problem that will probably never materialise.
